title: Graph Representations
summary: Adjacency lists, adjacency matrices, and edge lists encode the same graph with different space and lookup trade-offs. Pick the one that fits your graph's density and the operations you'll actually run.

slides.markdown:
A graph is just nodes and connections between them, but *how* you store those connections changes everything downstream — how fast you can check if an edge exists, how much memory you use, and how naturally your traversal code reads.

Three representations cover almost every interview and production case: **adjacency lists** (the default), **adjacency matrices** (O(1) edge lookup, O(V²) space), and **edge lists** (the flattest form, built for sorting). This topic is about picking correctly, not just knowing all three exist — the wrong choice under time or memory constraints is a real, recurring mistake.

slides.sectionTitle: Adjacency lists: the default for sparse graphs
slides.markdown:
An adjacency list stores, for every node, the list of nodes it directly connects to — typically a dictionary or array of lists, one entry per node. Space is O(V + E): you pay for exactly the edges that exist, nothing more.

This is the right default for the overwhelming majority of real graphs, because most real graphs are **sparse** — a social network with a million users doesn't have each user connected to all million others; a road network node connects to a handful of neighboring intersections, not every intersection in the city. Sparse means E is much closer to V than to V², and an adjacency list's cost scales with that reality.

slides.sectionTitle: Adjacency matrices: O(1) lookup, O(V²) space
slides.markdown:
An adjacency matrix is a V×V grid where `matrix[u][v]` is truthy (or holds a weight) exactly when an edge from `u` to `v` exists. Checking "is there an edge between u and v" is a single array access — O(1) — regardless of how many edges the graph has.

The cost is space: V² entries, allocated whether or not the edges exist. For V = 10,000 nodes, that's 100 million cells — fine if the graph is genuinely dense (most pairs connected), wasteful if it's sparse (most cells are unused zeros). The matrix also makes iterating "all of u's neighbors" cost O(V) — scan the whole row — even if u only has 2 real neighbors, which an adjacency list would give you directly in O(1) startup plus O(degree) to enumerate.

slides.sectionTitle: Edge lists: flattest form, built for sorting
slides.markdown:
An edge list is exactly what it sounds like: a flat list of `(u, v, weight)` tuples, one per edge, with no per-node structure at all. Space is O(E) — the leanest of the three — but it's the worst for anything that needs "give me u's neighbors," since that requires scanning the entire list.

Where it wins: algorithms that process edges **globally and by weight**, most notably Kruskal's MST algorithm, which needs to sort all edges once and then consider them in weight order — a structure organized per-node (list or matrix) doesn't help with that at all, while an edge list is already in exactly the right shape to sort.

<<< Image: a small graph with 4 nodes (A, B, C, D) and edges A-B, B-C, C-D, A-D drawn as a diagram on the left; on the right, three side-by-side boxes showing the same graph as (1) an adjacency list — A: [B, D], B: [A, C], C: [B, D], D: [A, C]; (2) a 4x4 adjacency matrix with 1s marking the four edges and 0s elsewhere; (3) an edge list — [(A,B), (B,C), (C,D), (A,D)] >>>

All three encode identical information — the picture should make clear that no representation is more "correct" than another; the choice is purely about which operations the algorithm you're about to run actually needs.

slides.sectionTitle: List vs matrix vs edge list
slides.markdown:
| | Adjacency list | Adjacency matrix | Edge list |
|---|---|---|---|
| Space | O(V + E) | O(V²) | O(E) |
| Edge existence check | O(degree) | O(1) | O(E) |
| Enumerate a node's neighbors | O(degree) | O(V) | O(E) |
| Best fit | Sparse graphs (most real graphs) | Dense graphs, or frequent edge-existence checks | Edge-sorting algorithms (Kruskal's) |

The row that surprises people: adjacency list neighbor enumeration is O(degree), not O(V) — you only ever touch a node's actual neighbors, which is the entire reason it wins on sparse graphs where degree is small relative to V.

slides.sectionTitle: Directed vs undirected: one entry or two
slides.markdown:
A **directed** edge from `u` to `v` means you can travel u → v but not necessarily v → u — store it once, in `u`'s adjacency list only. An **undirected** edge means the connection works both ways — store it twice, once in each endpoint's list (`graph[u].append(v)` and `graph[v].append(u)`), or once in a matrix cell pair `matrix[u][v] = matrix[v][u] = 1`.

The representation itself doesn't enforce this — it's purely a convention you apply consistently when building the graph. Mixing the convention (some edges mirrored, some not) inside one graph is a self-inflicted bug that surfaces as "my BFS says this node is unreachable" when it's actually just missing the return edge.

Not every graph problem hands you an explicit adjacency structure. A 2D grid (a maze, an image, a game board) is a graph where each cell is a node and its up-to-4 (or 8) neighbors are edges — but you never materialize an adjacency list for it. Instead, "get u's neighbors" is computed on the fly: `(r+1, c), (r-1, c), (r, c+1), (r, c-1)`, filtered against the grid's bounds.

Recognizing this is a graph problem at all — despite no `graph` variable existing anywhere — is the actual skill. BFS/DFS run exactly the same way on a grid as on an explicit adjacency list; only the neighbor-generation step changes.

slides.sectionTitle: Defaulting to a matrix and blowing the budget
slides.markdown:
The most common representation mistake: reaching for an adjacency matrix out of habit (it's simple to write, `matrix[u][v]`) on a graph that's actually sparse and large. A graph with 100,000 nodes needs a 100,000 × 100,000 matrix — 10 billion cells — which is not just slow to allocate, it typically won't fit in memory at all, even though the same graph might have only a few hundred thousand real edges and fit comfortably as an adjacency list.

The interview tell: before picking a representation, ask (out loud) roughly how many nodes and edges you're dealing with, and whether the graph is dense or sparse. That thirty seconds of calibration is what separates a considered choice from a reflexive one.

Building an undirected graph by only appending `graph[u].append(v)` and forgetting `graph[v].append(u)` is a bug that's easy to write and annoying to catch, because the graph still "works" — BFS from `u` finds `v` just fine. It only breaks when you traverse starting from `v` (or any node reachable only via that missing return edge), which frequently isn't the test case you happen to run first.

A reliable habit: write the edge-insertion helper once (as in the code slide above), have it handle the directed/undirected mirroring internally, and never manually append edges inline in algorithm code afterward.
